title: Microsoft and Amazon Chart Divergent Paths in the Battle for Cloud Gaming
excerpt: Xbox begins testing ad-supported game streaming for Insiders, while Amazon bets on bundling Luna with Prime to reach billions of casual players who don't own consoles.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Xbox Insiders can now stream owned games for free with preroll ads, in a test that could expand to all users soon.
  • Amazon has bundled nearly 100 games into Prime via Luna at no extra cost, targeting 2.5 billion casual players worldwide.
  • Both companies are pursuing the same underserved market — non-console gamers — but with opposite business models.
  • India, where Xbox Cloud Gaming starts at ₹499/month and Luna is included with Prime, is a key battleground for cloud gaming.
Divergent Strategies in Cloud Gaming

Bundled with Prime Subscription

Microsoft and Amazon are both making aggressive moves in cloud gaming — but their strategies could not look more different. On July 23, Xbox officially launched an ad-supported game streaming test with Xbox Insiders, while Amazon continues its quiet push to turn its Luna platform into a gaming gateway for hundreds of millions of Prime subscribers worldwide.

https://x.com/CaktusJxck/status/2080327788511265261

Xbox Opens Free Streaming With Ads

Microsoft announced on its Xbox Wire blog that Xbox Insiders can now stream games they own for free, supported by advertisements. The test, available across supported devices and regions, features preroll ads before sessions begin, with gameplay itself remaining uninterrupted. Sessions are capped at one hour.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OiUFgnkT_Qk

"When done well, advertising can help lower the cost of access. It creates another way for players to get into games without an upfront streaming purchase and expands audiences through new ways to play."

— Xbox Wire, Microsoft

The move has been months in the making. Internal testing began in late 2025, with employees able to stream select titles — including games they own, Free Play Days titles, and Xbox Retro Classics — after watching roughly two minutes of preroll ads. Reports from The Verge indicated sessions were capped at five free hours per month during internal trials, though Microsoft has not confirmed whether those limits will apply to the Insider test.

Microsoft laid out five principles for its approach to advertising in gaming: ads must create value for players, must not interrupt gameplay flow, must meet the same quality bar as content, must be clearly labelled, and must fit player expectations on each platform. The free tier will be available on PC, Xbox consoles, handheld devices, and web browsers.

Amazon's Prime-First Strategy

Amazon is pursuing a fundamentally different model. Under Jeff Gattis, a former Xbox executive who joined Amazon in 2025, the company has consolidated its fragmented gaming operations — Luna, Prime Gaming, and Amazon Game Studios — under one roof and abandoned any pretense of competing directly with PlayStation, Xbox, or Steam.

"We're not trying to compete with PlayStation or Xbox or Steam. That market's well served, if not overserved, today."

— Jeff Gattis, GM of Amazon Games

Instead, Amazon relaunched Luna in October 2025 as a Prime benefit, giving its hundreds of millions of Prime subscribers access to close to 100 games — including titles like Hogwarts Legacy, Indiana Jones, and EA Sports FC 26 — at no additional cost. The company is targeting the estimated 2.5 billion people worldwide who play games but do not own dedicated gaming hardware.

Gattis has been candid about the challenge. "You could argue that we're the largest paid gaming subscription in the world," he told Polygon in June. "Nobody knows they have it." Amazon is banking on its entertainment ecosystem — linking Luna with Prime Video, MGM franchises, Twitch, and upcoming game-and-TV pairings like Tomb Raider — to drive awareness.

Two Models, One Market Gap

Both companies are ultimately chasing the same underserved demographic: people who want to play games but will not or cannot invest in expensive hardware. The global cloud gaming market continues to expand as console and PC hardware costs climb, with high-end graphics cards now routinely exceeding $1,000 and next-generation consoles pushing toward four figures.

Microsoft's approach leans on its existing Xbox infrastructure and massive Game Pass library, betting that advertising revenue can subsidise free access and draw new players into its ecosystem. Amazon is wagering that Prime's built-in subscriber base — already paying for shipping, video, and music — represents a dormant gaming audience that just needs to discover it has access.

The India market illustrates the stakes. Xbox Cloud Gaming launched there in November 2025, making it Microsoft's 29th cloud gaming market, with plans starting at ₹499 per month. For a market where a single AAA game can cost ₹2,000-3,000 and a console runs ₹35,000-50,000, cloud streaming represents a genuine shift in accessibility. Amazon's Luna, bundled with Prime at no extra charge, offers an even lower barrier to entry.

What Comes Next

Microsoft says it will learn from the Insider test and iterate based on player feedback. The broader public rollout of ad-supported Xbox Cloud Gaming could arrive in the coming months. Amazon, meanwhile, is expanding Luna's game catalogue and leaning into AI-powered party games and cross-media IP plays, with Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis set for February 2027.

For now, the cloud gaming race has two distinct lanes: Microsoft is building a freemium funnel into Game Pass, while Amazon is quietly weaving gaming into the fabric of Prime. Which strategy wins may depend less on the games themselves and more on which company can reach the billions of potential players who have never picked up a controller.
